title: TB5-03222
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, the Appellant, alleges he is a citizen of Somalia and appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (a.k.a. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, the Appellant, alleges he is a citizen of Somalia and appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his claim for refugee protection. The Appellant asks that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) set aside the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) and substitute a decision with its own determination that the Appellant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. In the alternative, the Appellant requests that the RAD refer the matter back to the RPD with a differently constituted panel. The Appellant has submitted new evidence with the appeal as referred to in s.110(4) of the IRPA1 and requests an oral hearing be held pursuant to s.110(6) of the IRPA.
Pursuant to ss. 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD confirms the determination of the RPD and dismisses the appeal.

The Appellant alleged before the RPD that he was born in Qoryoley, Somalia on XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, into a family from the minority XXXX clan. On XXXX XXXX, 2009, Al-Shabab came to the family farm to collect produce. They told the Appellant's father that they need young boys to join their fight. The Appellant's father told them he was a Sufi and a peace lover. Al-Shabab became upset and shot the Appellant's father. They then asked the Appellant's mother where the Appellant was. She told them he was not at home.

The Appellant went into hiding at his uncle's home and he travelled to Addis Ababa, Ethiopia arriving on December 20, 2009. The Appellant remained in Ethiopia until April 1, 2011, when he departed for South Africa. He remained in South Africa for four months and then managed to fly to Brazil. He then travelled through numerous countries including Brazil, Panama and Mexico. He arrived in the United States (US), on February 22, 2013 and made an asylum claim at the border. On June 10, 2014, the Appellant met with his lawyer who told him his asylum claim would likely be denied. The lawyer advised the Appellant to go to Canada.

The Appellant crossed the border illegally on June 29, 2014. He was detained in Manitoba and subsequently made a refugee claim on October 9, 2014. The Appellant's refugee claim was heard on December 12, 2014 and February 4, 2015. In a decision of February 23, 2015, the RPD rejected the claim, finding that the Appellant was neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. The RPD further found that the Appellant had not established his identity and his credibility was seriously undermined by his testimony.
The Appellant submits the following issues: a) The RPD erred in its identity findings b) The RPD erred in its credibility findings ADMISSIBILITY OF NEW EVIDENCE PRESENTED ON APPEAL

As provided for in s. 110(3) of IRPA, with certain exceptions, the RAD must proceed without a hearing, on the basis of the record of the proceedings of the RPD and may accept documentary evidence and written submissions from the Minister and refugee claimant. Subsection 110(4) of IRPA provides that the person who is the subject of the appeal may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim or that was not reasonably available, or that the person could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to present, at the time of the rejection.

The Appellant has tendered four documents as proposed new evidence in support of his appeal: a) An affidavit from XXXX XXXX XXXX2 dated April 9, 2015 b) A letter from a former teacher, XXXX XXXX XXXX,3 dated March 25, 2015 c) A copy of a Marriage Certificate4 d) A letter from XXXX XXXX,5 a friend in South Africa.

In determining how the statutory provisions of Section 110(4) apply to this proposed new evidence, the RAD considered the following: Firstly, did the evidence arise after the rejection of the Appellant's refugee claim? * The RAD may consider whether the evidence is capable of proving the current state of affairs in the country of feared persecution, or an event that occurred or a circumstance that arose after the rejection of the refugee claim * The RAD will consider not only the date on which the document came into existence but the timing of the event or circumstance which the document seeks to prove. It is important to note here that Section 110(4) does not contemplate whether the evidence arose after the RPD's hearing but rather after the rejection of the Appellant's claim. * Where a document arose after the hearing but before the rejection of the refugee claim, it is necessary for the RAD to consider whether the Appellant could have presented the document to the RPD by way of a post-hearing submission. Secondly, if the RAD finds that the evidence did not arise after the rejection of the Appellant's refugee claim, it must consider the next factor in Section 110(4). * If the evidence is capable of proving only an event that occurred or circumstances that arose prior to the rejection, has the Appellant established that the evidence was not reasonably available for presentation to the RPD before it rejected the claim, or that it proves a fact that was unknown to him at the time of the hearing? Thirdly, if the RAD finds that the evidence did not arise after the rejection of the Appellant's refugee claim and that it was reasonably available at the time of the rejection, it must consider the final part of the Section 110(4) test: * Could the Appellant reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented the evidence prior to the rejection of his refugee claim? If so, the evidence need not be considered. If the Appellant could not reasonably have been expected to present the evidence to the RPD, the RAD will proceed to assess the credibility, relevance and materiality of the document.

In the case at hand, the Appellant submits he was unaware he had not provided sufficient evidence to establish his identity. The RAD finds that as much as these documents should have been available prior to the rejection of the Appellant's claim, the RAD accepts the Appellant's explanation that he would be unaware of the need to supply additional identity documentation. The RAD will admit the evidence under the requirements of s. 110(4). New Evidence Affidavit of XXXX XXXX XXXX

The Appellant submitted an affidavit6 from an individual who states that he met the Appellant in Qoryoley in 2007, while he was visiting his uncle. He further states that he encountered the Appellant in Mogadishu at a market in 2008. The Affiant submits the Appellant participated in Sufi customs and prayers at the mosque, he is "certain XXXX XXXX XXXX". He also states the name "XXXX" is given to members of the Ashraf clan and this is another reason to confirm his identity.

The RAD has reviewed the affidavit and notes the affiant is basing his identity statements on self-reported information provided by the Appellant. The Appellant's name, family information, clan identity and religious practices are all founded in information and actions of the Appellant.

The Affiant further relates that he learned about the death and the circumstances surrounding the death of the Appellant's father from an unidentified female trader in Somalia. The RAD finds this information is derived from an unconfirmed report obtained from a source which cannot be verified or confirmed.

The RAD notes in assessing the content of the affidavit that the RPD in its Reasons has accepted that the Appellant was the individual XXXX XXXX , who was last present in Somalia in 2009. The RAD finds the affidavit submitted does not allow the affiant to confirm the Appellant's identity as a national of Somalia. The RAD notes the Appellant could also be the child of one or both parents who were of Somali heritage, but born and raised elsewhere. The RAD finds as much as the affiant states that the Appellant speaks the Somali language, has the appearance and actions of a member of the Ashraf clan, the affidavit provides no additional evidence which would allow the RAD to confirm his identity as a Somali national. The teacher's letter

The Appellant has submitted a letter received in an email from a former childhood teacher. RAD has reviewed the letter and notes there is no documentation contained in the submission to ascertain the origin of this letter. The RAD notes the copy is not a sworn affidavit, nor is it notarized. The RAD further notes as much as the author of the letter states he is a teacher from a XXXX XXXX in Qoryoley, there is no supporting documentation to ascertain this statement. The RAD also notes the document is not produced on any form of school letterhead. The RAD finds it reasonable to expect that an individual who states he is a teacher from a XXXX XXXX would produce his letter on school letterhead or in the least, provide some form of corroborating documentation. The RAD further notes that the Appellant's testimony was that he attended school sporadically for a total of four years, the last time being in 2004.

The RAD further finds the author makes a series of statements about the incidents associated with the Appellant that consist of knowledge he has gained through reporting from the Appellant or his family members. The author speaks of attending the Appellant's father's burial and speaking to two relatives from whom he obtained much of the information which he relates in the letter. The RAD notes the author in his letter does not confirm speaking with or seeing the Appellant on the day of the burial. The RAD finds the information related in the letter is founded in second or third hand information.

The RAD finds it is unable to substantiate the identity of the writer of the document or its provenance. In considering the concerns the RAD has identified and assessing the information it provides, the RAD places little evidentiary weight on the contents of the letter. If the RAD were to place any weight on this letter, the RAD finds it simply places the Appellant in Somalia in the year 2004. The RAD further finds this letter cannot be relied upon to substantiate the Appellant's identity as a national of Somalia. The letter from XXXX XXXX

The Appellant has submitted a letter7 from the individual he alleges he lived with for the four month period he was in South Africa. The RAD notes the letter is not original, but the Appellant submits it is a copy of a document derived from an e-mail. The RAD notes there is no documentation contained in the submission to ascertain the origin of this letter. The RAD further notes the copy is not a sworn affidavit, nor is it notarized. The RAD is unable to confirm the identity of the author or the provenance of the document. The RAD places little evidentiary weight on this document. The marriage certificate
The original marriage certificate was submitted under a Rule 29(2) Application and the document is addressed in the following section. Application to submit documents not previously provided

The Appellant submitted an application under Rule 29(2) of the Refugee protection Division Rules. In his application, the Appellant submits documents which he argues provide evidence that the Appellant was working and that he was married in Ethiopia and that this refutes the credibility findings in respect of his time in Ethiopia at the RPD hearing.

The Appellant has submitted the following documents with his application: a) An original marriage certificate8 dated XXXX XXXX, 2010. b) A copy of a letter printed from an email dated June 1, 2015, which indicates that the Appellant was working two days per week for four months in 2010 in Ethiopia.

The RAD has considered these documents, pursuant to the factors in Rule 29(4). Section 29(4) of the RAD Rules states that: 4.) In deciding whether to allow an application, the Division must consider any relevant factors, including a) the document's relevance and probative value; b) any new evidence the document brings to the appeal; and c) whether the person who is the subject of the appeal, with reasonable effort, could have provided the document or written submissions with the appellant's record, respondent's record or reply record.

With regard to the marriage certificate, the RAD notes that the Appellant has previously submitted a copy of the document. He states the original document was not available at the time he submitted his appeal. The RAD finds this document is admissible as additional evidence in this appeal.

In respect of the copy of the letter from co-worker in Ethiopia, the RAD finds the letter has been submitted in an attempt to confirm aspects of the Appellant's testimony. The RAD will admit the copy of the letter as additional evidence in this appeal. The marriage certificate

The Appellant has submitted this document as support for his testimony about his time spent in Ethiopia and the RPD's inquiry about his ability to document his stay in that country. The RAD has reviewed the record as well as the audio recording of the hearing. The RAD notes the Appellant testified that he was married in Ethiopia in the summer of 2010 in a "religious ceremony", stating that he could not afford a formal wedding with a reception. The RAD notes this would imply there was no civil record of the marriage. The RAD further notes the document states the marriage took place on XXXX XXXX, 2010, leading the RAD to question the credibility of the Appellant's testimony in this issue.

The RAD in assessing the genuineness of the document notes that they are produced on embossed paper and appears to be printed in a format that could be reproduced with any basic word processing program. The RAD notes the document has been produced without any security features. The RAD further notes when examining the print on this document there appears to be additional print or shadowing of another font in the background indicating this document may have been reprinted at some point in the production process. The RAD finds it reasonable to believe that the authorities in Ethiopia would not issue an official document with visible printing flaws.

In addition the document contains two ink stamps. The RAD notes there is a signature as well as the official's printed name on the document in the area of the stamps. The RAD notes that this information is written over the stamp. The purpose of a stamp is to "seal" the document to attest to its genuineness and as a means to demonstrate that it has not been altered or tampered with. The presence of data written over a seal undermines the integrity of the stamp and as a result, the credibility of the document itself.

As well the RAD notes no samples of these documents are available in the IRB national documentation country documents for comparison to valid original documents. The RAD further notes the Appellant through his oral testimony in respect of his travel through multiple countries has demonstrated he is not adverse to obtaining and utilizing fraudulent documents. Further to this, the RAD notes the documentary evidence9 confirms that fraudulent documents are readily available to refugee claimants from Somalia.
The RAD is led to conclude the claimant has the means and ability to secure duplicitous documentation to assist in his quest for refugee protection in Canada.

The RAD notes that where there is sufficient evidence to cast doubt on a document's authenticity, whether because of an irregularity on its face or the questionable circumstances in which it was obtained or provided, a document may be assigned little (or no) weight, without expert verification or where such verification is inconclusive.10 The RAD also notes that submitting a false or irregular document may have an impact on the weight assigned to other documents provided by the claimant, especially when they are interrelated,11 and on the overall credibility of a claimant.12

With this information in in mind, considering the facts and documentary evidence surrounding the Appellant's document presented in evidence, the panel places little evidentiary weight on the marriage certificate presented as support in this claim. The RAD further finds that this finding severely undermines the credibility of the Appellant in respect of his testimony about his marriage, his presence in Ethiopia and his allegations of persecution in Somalia. The letter from a colleague

The Appellant has also submitted a letter from a fellow worker at a XXXX in Dirdawa, Ethiopia, where he was allegedly employed two days per week for a period of four months in 2010. The RAD in examining the letter notes it is not an original document and the accompanying document indicates it was attached to an e-mail. The RAD further notes the e-mail address does not identify any association with the author of the letter. The RAD notes the document is not a sworn or notarized affidavit. The RAD has no means to identify the author or verify the origin of the document. The RAD additionally notes the document does not specify the actual months the Appellant was employed in the year 2010. The RAD has also considered the author of the letter states he was in Dirdawa when the Appellant left Ethiopia. The RAD notes he does not identify the date of this occurrence or how he came to be aware of the information. The RAD finds this statement makes little sense considering the Appellant has stated in his BoC document13 that he left Ethiopia in April 2011, a considerable time after allegedly being employed at the XXXX.

The RAD notes the audio recording of the hearing indicates the Appellant was confronted by the RPD at the hearing in respect of statements made in his BoC document, which identified that he resided in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia from December 2009 until April 2011. The RPD at the hearing and in its Reasons noted there was no mention of this in any of his immigration forms completed through his refugee claim process of residing in Dirdawa, Ethiopia. The Appellant testified that he did not list all of the locations where he lived while there, but offered no salient explanation as to why he chose not to provide accurate residency information to the Immigration and Refugee Board in respect of this eighteen month period of residency in Ethiopia.

The RAD in assessing the credibility issues surrounding the issuing of the letter as well as its contents and considering the Appellant's testimony and documentation of his sojourn in Ethiopia, places little evidentiary weight on the letter.

The RAD finds that neither of the two documents submitted are sufficient to confirm the Appellant's statements that he resided in Ethiopia following his alleged departure from Somalia in December 2009.

Counsel has made submissions in regard to the role that the RAD plays in the review of an RPD decision. However, the RAD finds that the recent Federal Court decision in Huruglica,14 provides the RAD with guidance in relation to the appropriate standard that must be applied by the RAD to decisions of the RPD. Justice Phelan states in paragraphs 54 and 55 of the foregoing decision: [54] Having concluded that the RAD erred in reviewing the RPD's decision on the standard of reasonableness, I have further concluded that for the reasons above, the RAD is required to conduct a hybrid appeal. It must review all aspects of the RPD's decision and come to an independent assessment of whether the claimant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. Where its assessment departs from that of the RPD, the RAD must substitute its own decision. [55] In conducting its assessment, it can recognize and respect the conclusion of the RPD on such issues as credibility and/or where the RPD enjoys a particular advantage in reaching such a conclusion but it is not restricted, as an appellate court is, to intervening on facts only where there is an "overriding and palpable error".

While there has been some conflict in the case law from the Federal Court regarding the standard of review to be applied by the RAD when reviewing RPD decisions, Justice Martineau in Alyafi15 has said that, in the face of this conflict, the Federal Court should allow the RAD to apply either approach as long as the question of the scope of the appellate review of the RPD's decisions has not been settled by a final judgment by the Federal Court of Appeal or the Supreme Court of Canada.

Accordingly, the RAD will conduct its own assessment of the RPD's decision and come to an independent assessment of whether the Appellant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. Deference will be afforded to the credibility findings of the RPD or to other findings where the RPD has a particular advantage in reaching its conclusions. ANALYSIS OF THE MERITS OF THE APPEAL No presumption of article 1E in law

The RPD found the Appellant may have been present in Somalia, but he had not established that he was a national of Somalia, where he had travelled and whether he has obtained citizenship or status in some other country. The Appellant submits this amounts to unsubstantiated speculation and that the RPD has presumed that Article 1E applies automatically and it is up to the Appellant to prove otherwise. The RAD is not persuaded by this argument.

The RAD has reviewed the record and notes the RPD has based its findings on the testimony of the claimant as well as the documentation submitted in this claim. The RAD finds the Appellant has taken the statements of the RPD out of context. At no point in reviewing the audio recording of the hearing or its Reasons does the RAD find that the RPD stated or implied that exclusion under Article 1E is being considered as an issue in the claim or that it was necessary for the Appellant to prove that he had not acquired status in other countries.

The Appellant further submits the RPD has erred in impugning his credibility as to his identity because he could not corroborate his testimony about the countries he had travelled through in order to get to Canada. The RAD has reviewed the record and finds the Appellant's own evidence and sworn testimony raised the credibility concerns surrounding his travel to Canada. For example the RAD finds issues arise around the Appellant's testimony around his extended time spent residing in Ethiopia. He testified that he had lived in a number of locations while he was in Ethiopia. When he was confronted by the RPD as to why he did not list these locations in any of the documents associated with his claim for refugee protection, he indicated that he travelled through many countries in Central America, but he did not provide all the details on them. The RAD finds his response was designed to minimize the importance of the issue, but it notes he did not address the question as put to him. The RAD finds the Appellant's response detracts from his ability to act as a credible witness.

The RAD further notes the Appellant provided contradictory testimony about the location of his family members and his ties to Ethiopia to US authorities. In addition he provided inconsistent testimony in respect of his travel to Canada when compared to his BoC and other documents. The RAD finds it reasonable to believe that the Appellant having resided for an extended time in countries where he worked and interacted with various individuals would provide some form of documentation of his residency there. The RAD having reviewed the record finds the Appellant's own evidence raised the possibility of potential status in other locations. The Appellant argues that the RPD ignored the Appellant's sworn testimony in respect of his travel and in doing so violates the principles set out in Maldonado.16 The RAD finds that in Maldonado, the court states, in part, "When an applicant swears to the truth of certain allegations, this creates a presumption that those allegations are true unless there be reason to doubt their truthfulness."17
The RAD finds that concerns surrounding the Appellant's credibility negate the presumption of truthfulness associated with the Appellant's sworn testimony.

The RAD finds it was well within the purview of the RPD to explore these issues in arriving at its determination in this claim. The RAD finds it agrees with the conclusion of the RPD and the Appellant's argument must fail. Identity Witnesses

The RPD found that the Appellant's identity witnesses were unable to establish that the Appellant is a national of Somalia. The Appellant submits that the RPD reasons for discounting the evidence of Mr. XXXX are inadequate. The Appellant further submits that the totality of the evidence of both witnesses establishes the Appellant's personal and national identity. The RAD is not persuaded by this argument.

The RAD in reviewing the audio recording of the hearing notes the first witness Mr. XXXX alleges he is related to the Appellant, but his testimony in respect of establishing the identity of the Appellant was vague and lacking in credibility. The witness testified that he left Somalia in 1990 (the Appellant would have been approximately three years old). He testified that he had discussions about the Appellant and his presence in Canada with the Appellant's mother, prior to encountering the Appellant in Canada.

During questioning by the RPD, the witness was asked to describe what he and the Appellant discussed during their meetings. The witness was vague in his response. For example he stated they discussed, "who the target was at home". He was asked for additional detail as to whom the target is and he replied, "People with different religious beliefs". The RAD finds the responses of the witness lacked specific detail and was hesitant. The witness was asked if he and the Appellant discussed why he left Somalia. He responded, "No we did not go as deeply as that". The RAD notes the witness was aware of very little personal information about the Appellant. For example he was unaware of the Appellant's mother's full name, what the Appellant's religious affiliation was or whether he was married.

The witness was later questioned as to whether the Appellant had specifically told him why he left Somalia. He replied, "No, but I know why". He was asked to explain and he again provided a vague, non-specific reply, "He is from the group that spreads religion and they don't like that". The witness was subsequently asked if he was aware of where the Appellant's father is. The RAD notes the witness was non-responsive and the question was put to him three times before he responded indicating his father was dead. When asked how he was aware of this he stated that the Appellant's mother told him.

The RAD in reviewing the record finds that Mr. XXXX provided no persuasive evidence to support that he was related to the Appellant. Further to this the RAD finds Mr. XXXX testimony was lacking in credibility. Additionally the RAD finds, on a balance of probabilities, that any information that he had acquired in reference to the Appellant's identity and circumstances in Somalia could have been acquired in conversation with others.

In respect of the second identity witness, Mr. XXXX, the RAD in reviewing the audio recording of his exchange with the RPD notes his testimony was also vague and lacking in specific detail. The Appellant testified that he and the witness spoke every day since meeting in Canada. The RPD questioned the Appellant about how much time he and the witness spoke in Canada, as well as what they spoke about. The RAD finds the Appellant's responses to this inquiry were vague and evasive. The RAD notes that both the Appellant and the witness were able to relate an encounter with the Appellant in Somalia in the year 2005. The witness then noted that he saw the Appellant again in 2009 in Somalia. The RAD additionally notes Mr. XXXX was able to provide few personal details about the Appellant's family or the Appellant when they were young, beyond a common interest in soccer.

The RAD notes the witness was questioned as to what he and the Appellant discussed when they talked in Canada. The RAD finds his responses were hesitant and at times evasive, often requiring prompting from the RPD. The RPD asked the witness about his age when he met the Appellant and his answer and the Appellant's answer were not the same. When he was asked to explain why, he answered, "Somali people don't discuss tribe and age". The RAD finds the Appellant's responses when questioned about distinctive features about the town in which he and the Appellant lived in Somalia were equally hesitant and vague.

The RAD, in considering the testimony of the witness finds that the witness and the Appellant had indeed encountered each other in Somalia and shared common interest in soccer, but little more. The RAD notes it was of interest that the witness was able to relate information about the Appellant's father and the problems with Al-Shabab despite being able to provide limited information about the Appellant's family beyond this issue. The RAD, in considering the vague and evasive testimony provided by the Appellant and Mr. XXXX in reference to their discussions in Canada, finds this information could have been provided by the Appellant in the course of the Canadian conversations. The RAD places little weight on the testimony about the Appellant's father. The RAD further finds Mr. XXXX did not provide persuasive testimony to confirm the Appellant's identity as a national of Somalia. The RAD finds upon its review of the testimony of the identity witnesses it agrees with the finding of the RPD. Additional Identity Evidence

The Appellant submits that the RPD failed to have regard for other forms of evidence submitted in support of his identity. These documents include the Appellant's US claim documents,18 a letter from the Somali Center of Kansas City (SCKCM),19 a letter from Somali Immigrant Aid Organization (SIAO)20 and a document from the Appellant's mother.21 The RAD in reviewing the Reasons from this claim finds the RPD does state that it considered all of the evidence, but it only refers to the evidence in its Reasons that is relevant to its decision. The RAD is not persuaded by the argument of the Appellant.
The RAD has independently reviewed and assessed these documents as well as the audio recording of the hearing.

In respect of the Appellant's US claim documents, the Appellant in his interview with US authorities stated that he held a legally issued Somali passport. Yet when confronted by the RPD about these statements he stated that the document was a Somali passport obtained from the smuggler and it only contained his picture. The RAD finds the Appellant's testimony provided in his Record of Sworn Statement in Proceedings document, was lacking in credibility. The RAD in reviewing this document finds no persuasive evidence that the Appellant provided any genuine documents to US authorities in order to establish his identity.

In respect of the letters from the Somali Center of Kansas City (SCKCM), the RAD on reviewing this document notes the document from the SCKCM states the two individuals listed in the document stated to the author of the letter that they were aware of the facts stated therein. The RAD finds the letter does not indicate how these individuals came to be aware of this information. The RAD places little weight on this document as proof of the Appellant's identity.

In respect of the letter from the Somali Immigrant Aid Organization (SIAO), the RAD on reviewing this document notes it is based on a self-reported interview with the Appellant and the author's observations from the interview. The RAD finds this letter is not founded in any documented fact, but it is simply the author's opinion about the Appellant. The RAD places little evidentiary weight on this document in establishing the identity of the Appellant.

The RAD reviewed the affidavit from the Appellant's mother and notes it states the Appellant is her son and that his father was killed in Somalia. The RAD finds the document confirms the Appellant's name, but it does not serve to establish his identity as a national of Somalia.

The RAD has reviewed the Appellant's additional documents submitted in support of his identity and finds they provide no additional persuasive support in establishing the Appellant's identity as a national of Somalia. Credibility Findings Who Does the Appellant Fear?

The RPD found the Appellant's testimony as to the reasons he left Somalia were inconsistent in respect of the information provided in his US and Canadian refugee claims and this undermines his ability to act as a credible witness. The Appellant submits he provided a reasonable explanation to the RPD. The RAD is not persuaded by the argument of the Appellant.

The RAD notes the Appellant was confronted by the RPD at the first sitting of his claim about the inconsistency in his statements to US authorities as to how his father was killed in Somalia. The RPD explained to the claimant that his testimony in the US Record of Sworn Statement in Proceedings document22 does not mention the words Al-Shabab anywhere. The RPD further noted that the US document stated that his father was killed by "local people who were fighting over a farm his father owned". The Appellant was asked to explain why he did not tell the US authorities his father was killed by Al-Shabab as was his evidence in his Canadian claim. The Appellant replied stating, "I did (tell them) when I said they are local people". The RAD does not find the description "local people" provides any linkage to Al-Shabab. He later modified his testimony to state, "A man who came from Mogadishu...claimed my father's farm was his and they got in a fight and they killed my father". The RAD finds the Appellant's later testimony does not indicate that this individual is a "local person".

The RAD notes the Appellant was questioned directly by the US authorities about Al-Shabab and he denied any interaction with them. The Appellant answered in the negative when asked by US authorities if any terrorist organization had attempted to recruit him. The RPD asked the Appellant if at the time he made his US asylum claim if he was afraid of Al-Shabab. He hesitated and eventually answered, "Yes". The RPD noted for the Appellant that he did not mention Al-Shabab at any point in his US testimony and asked him to explain why. The Appellant was evasive and attempted to avoid providing a response.

During the second sitting of his claim, the Appellant during questioning by his counsel was asked why did not mention Al-Shabab in his US Record of Sworn Statement in Proceedings interview. He answered, "I was told by other Somalis not to mention Al-Shabab or I would be deported". The RAD further finds it is reasonable to believe if this was the situation the Appellant would have provided this testimony during the first sitting of his claim during the two occasions he was questioned about it. The RAD recalls the words of the Federal Court in reference to the assessment of testimony. A person's first story is usually the most genuine and, therefore, the one to be most believed. That being said, although the failure to report a fact can be a cause for concern, it should not always be so. That, again depends on all the circumstances: see Fajardo v. Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration), [1993] F.C.J. No. 915 at para. 5 (QL) (C.A.); Owusu-Ansah, supra; and Sheikh v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [2000] F.C.J. No. 568 (QL) (T.D.).23

The RAD notes the Appellant was given multiple opportunities to provide his latter testimony during the first sitting of his claim and he consciously chose not to do so. The RAD finds the Appellant's testimony on this issue evolved throughout his RPD hearing. The RAD finds the Appellant's evolving testimony was an attempt to offset his previous inconsistent testimony. The RAD finds the Appellant's latter explanation is lacking in credibility and undermines the basis of his claim for refugee protection. The RAD agrees with the finding of the RPD in this area. The Appellant's argument must fail. The Minor Inconsistencies

The Appellant submits that the RPD engaged in a series of negative credibility findings based on microscopic examination. The Appellant further submits that these issues are minor in nature and are not material to the core issues of the claim. The Appellant's marriage

The Appellant submits that he testified during the RPD hearing that he was married in the summer of 2010 in Ethiopia. The Appellant further testified that the US authorities made a mistake in identifying this wife as his fiancée. The Appellant submits that the RPD has used the Appellant's failure to supply supporting documentation in his claim as a method of impugning the Appellant's credibility. The RAD notes the Appellant submitted the original marriage license as new evidence in this appeal as support for his identity and his presence in Ethiopia. The RAD has previously addressed credibility concerns associated with the authenticity of this document. The RAD in considering the finding associated with the marriage certificate further finds that the Appellant's testimony that the US authorities made a mistake is not credible. The location of the Appellant's family

The RPD found the Appellant's testimony regarding the location of his family was inconsistent in respect of the information provided in his US and Canadian refugee claims and this further undermines his ability to act as a credible witness. The Appellant submits that the US translator made a mistake in his US testimony. The Appellant further submits that this is a minor error and the RPD microscopically relied on the US interview notes. The RAD is not persuaded by the findings of the RPD on this issue.

The RAD has reviewed the audio recording of the hearing and notes the Appellant's US interview document was the source of multiple inconsistencies such as this. The RAD further notes that in its review of the Appellant's testimony in respect of the Appellant's testimony surrounding his US Record of Sworn Statement in Proceedings interview,24 the Appellant acknowledged there were many "mistakes". The Appellant was confronted by the RPD during his testimony at various points and asked to explain these inconsistencies. In every circumstance, the Appellant blamed the inconsistencies on mistakes made by the US authorities.

The RAD has examined the document and notes the Appellant was asked if there was any additional information in the US interview that he cared to add. The Appellant also signed a declaration stating that he read the document following the interview, acknowledging that the contents were true and correct. The RAD further notes that the Appellant at the outset of his hearing before the RPD was provided with an opportunity to amend his documents. The RAD finds if the Appellant was aware of inconsistencies in this document he was given multiple opportunities to correct the information.

Additionally the RAD finds the Appellant's statement that his interview with US immigration officials was not accurate lacks credibility. The interview was conducted by officers of the US Department of Justice, Immigration and Naturalization Service in accordance with specific protocols and the Appellant has adduced no persuasive evidence to indicate they are not acting in accordance with these protocols. The RAD finds the Appellant's explanation for these inconsistencies is not credible.

A further example arises when the Appellant is confronted by the RPD about his testimony in respect to his employment in Ethiopia and later in South Africa. The Appellant testified in his Canadian hearing that he did omit the employment information from his IMM5669 document because, "This is not a job". The RAD notes when he was questioned by US authorities about his employment, the Appellant clearly identifies his work in Ethiopia and South Africa. The RAD finds the Appellant's explanation before the RPD in this matter is simply not credible.

The Appellant argues that this was a minor inconsistency. The RAD disagrees with this argument by the Appellant. The Appellant has alleged he has travelled through these various countries in order to escape persecution in Somalia. The RAD notes that the Appellant spent extended periods of time in a number of countries that are signatories to the UN Convention on Refugees. The RAD finds that the Appellant's presence and activities in these countries are key components of his claim for refugee protection.

A further situation arose when the Appellant was questioned about his travels following his departure from Ethiopia. The Appellant confirmed his statements from his US documents that he transited through Sudan and Mozambique for two months. The RPD noted that his IMM0008 form did not mention these two countries as part of his journey to Canada. The Appellant's explanation was that these were "transit" countries. The RAD finds this explanation makes little sense when one considers that the Appellant spent more time in these countries than some of the South American countries he listed in his documents.

The Appellant further submits that the RPD finding in respect to the actual location of his mother and siblings is a minor issue and amounts to a microscopic examination of the evidence. The RAD does not agree with the argument of the Appellant. The RAD finds that the current country of residence of the Appellant's family is an important and relevant factor in the assessment of the Appellant's identity as well as the credibility of his allegations.

The RAD has considered the Appellant's argument that some of these inconsistencies and contradictions when viewed as singular credibility findings could be regarded as not being material to the core issues of the claim. The RAD has reviewed a number of these findings and finds this assessment of the Appellant's testimony and evidence is not microscopic. The RAD finds these concerns are not founded on minor issues, but provide information which is central to the core elements of the claim. The RAD finds the argument of the Appellant must fail.

With regard to the credibility of the evidence that the Appellant has submitted, the RAD refers to the sentiment expressed in the case of Dan-Ash that: ... unless one is prepared to postulate (and accept) unlimited credulity on the part of the Board, there must come a point at which a witness's contradictions will move even the most generous trier of fact to reject his evidence.25

As well the RAD notes in Sheikh,26 MacGuigan, J.A., writing for the court, stated, in part:, "In other words a general finding of a lack of credibility on the part of the applicant may conceivably extend to all relevant information emanating from his testimony."

The RAD finds when one assesses the cumulative effect of the numerous credibility issues arising from the Appellant's testimony and the accompanying documentation, these findings lead the RAD to conclude the Appellant has failed to act as a credible witness.

According to Section 110(6), the RAD may hold a hearing if, in its opinion, there is documentary evidence referred to in 110(3) that raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the Appellant, that is central to the RPD's decision, and that, if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim. In this appeal, where there is no evidence from or in response to the Minister, the documentary evidence referred to in Section 110(3) must be understood in relation to Section 110(4).

When read together, Sections 110(3), (4), and (6) establish that the RAD must not hold a hearing in an appeal such as this unless there is new (Section 110(4)) evidence, in which case the RAD may hold a hearing if that new evidence raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the Appellant, is central to the RPD's decision, and that, if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim.

The Appellant has submitted no new evidence in support of his appeal that raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the Appellant or that is central to the RPD's decision, and would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim. As such, the RAD must proceed without a hearing on the basis of the RPD's record, and his application for an oral hearing is denied. Summary

The RAD has reviewed the submissions of the Appellant as well as all of the evidence in this claim. The RAD has found: * The Appellant failed to act as a credible witness in his quest for refugee protection. * The Appellant may have resided in Somalia at some time during his life. The Appellant was last identified in Somalia in 2009. * The Appellant was unable to provide persuasive evidence that he is a national of Somalia or any other country.

Pursuant to Section 111(1)(a) of IRPA, the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. Accordingly, this appeal is dismissed.
